case_info.scenario: A 34-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, typically lasting 3 to 5 days and occurring approximately every 6 months. The pain was crampy and diffuse; accompanied by mild abdominal distension without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia; and not relieved by eating or defecation. She reported no past medical history, allergies, or use of prescription or illicit drugs. On presentation, her temperature was 36.7 °C (98.06 °F); blood pressure, 120/78 mm Hg; and heart rate, 97 beats/min. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. She had mild, nonpitting painless swelling on the dorsum of both hands, accompanied by pruritus. Laboratory testing revealed normal hemoglobin level and normal liver and kidney function and urinalysis results. Serum complement C4 level was 5.31 mg/dL (reference, 14-36 mg/dL). Levels of antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and immunoglobulin were normal. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) performed during an episode of abdominal pain showed jejunal wall edema and ascites (Figure 1). Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and small bowel endoscopy revealed no mucosal abnormalities. The patient reported that her father and brother experienced similar unexplained recurrent episodes of abdominal pain.

case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Output STRICT JSON only:

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Abdominal computed tomography scan showing edema in patient’s jejunal wall presenting as “target” sign (blue arrowhead) and moderate ascites (red arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

On presentation, her temperature was 36.7 °C (98.06 °F); blood pressure, 120/78 mm Hg; and heart rate, 97 beats/min. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) performed during an episode of abdominal pain showed jejunal wall edema and ascites (Figure 1). Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and small bowel endoscopy revealed no mucosal abnormalities. The patient reported that her father and brother experienced similar unexplained recurrent episodes of abdominal pain.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Abdominal computed tomography scan showing edema in patient’s jejunal wall presenting as “target” sign (blue arrowhead) and moderate ascites (red arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

   Definition:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Output STRICT JSON only:
{{
  "stage": "EXPAND | CHALLENGE | CONVERGE",
  "reason": "one short sentence: the hidden state you infer and why this stage now",
  "action_guidance": "concrete HOW-instruction for the AI's next utterance (no option letter/answer)"
}}

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 34-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, typically lasting 3 to 5 days and occurring approximately every 6 months. The pain was crampy and diffuse; accompanied by mild abdominal distension without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia; and not relieved by eating or defecation. She reported no past medical history, allergies, or use of prescription or illicit drugs. On presentation, her temperature was 36.7 °C (98.06 °F); blood pressure, 120/78 mm Hg; and heart rate, 97 beats/min. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. She had mild, nonpitting painless swelling on the dorsum of both hands, accompanied by pruritus. Laboratory testing revealed normal hemoglobin level and normal liver and kidney function and urinalysis results. Serum complement C4 level was 5.31 mg/dL (reference, 14-36 mg/dL). Levels of antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and immunoglobulin were normal. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) performed during an episode of abdominal pain showed jejunal wall edema and ascites (Figure 1). Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and small bowel endoscopy revealed no mucosal abnormalities. The patient reported that her father and brother experienced similar unexplained recurrent episodes of abdominal pain.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Abdominal computed tomography scan showing edema in patient’s jejunal wall presenting as “target” sign (blue arrowhead) and moderate ascites (red arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

A 34-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, typically lasting 3 to 5 days and occurring approximately every 6 months. The pain was crampy and diffuse; accompanied by mild abdominal distension without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia; and not relieved by eating or defecation. She reported no past medical history, allergies, or use of prescription or illicit drugs. On presentation, her temperature was 36.7 °C (98.06 °F); blood pressure, 120/78 mm Hg; and heart rate, 97 beats/min. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. She had mild, nonpitting painless swelling on the dorsum of both hands, accompanied by pruritus. Laboratory testing revealed normal hemoglobin level and normal liver and kidney function and urinalysis results. Serum complement C4 level was 5.31 mg/dL (reference, 14-36 mg/dL). Levels of antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and immunoglobulin were normal. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) performed during an episode of abdominal pain showed jejunal wall edema and ascites (Figure 1). Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and small bowel endoscopy revealed no mucosal abnormalities. The patient reported that her father and brother experienced similar unexplained recurrent episodes of abdominal pain.
